Teach me to fix my gaze, and let my focused hours today be an offering to you. <break time="1.1s" /> I will give my best work one unbroken hour of full attention today. <break time="1.1s" /> Go into the day with your eyes straight ahead, held by the One whose eyes never leave you. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-w-busyness: On Busyness and Fruit. <break time="1.8s" /> You were in motion all week. Sit still long enough to ask what actually grew. <break time="1.1s" /> “I am the vine; you are the branches. If you remain in me and I in you, you will bear much fruit; apart from me you can do nothing.” <break time="1.1s" />John 15:5. <break time="1.1s" /> Busyness is the most respectable way to be unfruitful. A packed calendar looks like progress, feels like importance, and quietly excuses you from the harder question: is any of this bearing fruit? Founders know the difference in their gut — the week of forty meetings that moved nothing, versus the one quiet morning that changed the company. Jesus doesn’t tell the branches to try harder. He tells them to remain. Fruit, in his picture, is not manufactured by activity; it grows out of connection. A branch straining on its own produces motion, heat, exhaustion — everything but grapes. “Apart from me you can do nothing” is not a scolding; it’s a mercy, because it releases you from the lie that output is generated by sheer velocity. So audit the week the way a gardener would, not the way a timesheet would. What is actually growing — in the product, in your people, in you? Cut one busy thing that bears nothing. Keep the connected things. God is not impressed by your fullest day; he is at work in your fruitful one, and fruit comes from abiding first. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, I have mistaken a full schedule for a faithful life. Show me which of my busyness is just motion. Keep me connected to you, the vine, and let what grows from my work this week be real fruit, not noise. <break time="1.1s" /> I will cut one fruitless commitment this week and stay rooted in what actually grows. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and remain in the vine, and let the fruit come from there. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-w-procrastination: On Putting It Off. <break time="1.8s" /> There it sits, third day on the list — the task you keep organizing around instead of doing. <break time="1.1s" /> “Whoever watches the wind will not plant; whoever looks at the clouds will not reap.” <break time="1.1s" />Ecclesiastes 11:4. <break time="1.1s" /> Procrastination almost never looks like laziness in a founder. It looks like research. It looks like tidying the roadmap, answering easier emails, waiting for the right moment to make the hard call or send the scary draft. Ecclesiastes names the pattern with unsettling precision: the farmer who keeps watching the wind never actually plants anything. He isn’t idle — he’s studying conditions. But the conditions are never quite right, and study has quietly become a place to hide. Under most procrastination sits fear: of doing it badly, of finding out, of being judged by the result. Here is where the gospel loosens the knot. You are not waiting on a perfect performance to be acceptable; you are already accepted, which makes the imperfect first attempt survivable. The draft can be rough. The call can be awkward. Planting is an act of faith precisely because you can’t control the weather — that part has always belonged to God. So name the one task you’ve been circling, and do it first, before the day offers you its usual hiding places. Plant the seed. Let God handle the wind. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, you know the task I’ve been avoiding and the fear underneath it. Forgive me for hiding in busywork. Give me the small courage to begin badly rather than wait perfectly, and take charge of the outcomes I can’t control. <break time="1.1s" /> I will do the avoided task first today, before I touch anything easier. <break time="1.1s" /> Go plant today what you have been watching the wind about. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-w-priorities: On the One Thing. <break time="1.8s" /> Forty items, all marked urgent. Before you triage the list, let the Lord quiet the room. <break time="1.1s" /> “Martha, Martha,” the Lord answered, “you are worried and upset about many things, but few things are needed — or indeed only one. Mary has chosen what is better, and it will not be taken away from her.” <break time="1.1s" />Luke 10:41–42. <break time="1.1s" /> Notice that Jesus doesn’t rebuke Martha for working. He names what the work has done to her: worried and upset about many things. That’s the founder’s condition most mornings — not too little to do but too many things claiming to be the thing, until the day is spent reacting and nothing essential moves. Jesus’ answer is almost shockingly narrow: few things are needed, or indeed only one. Mary’s one thing was his presence, and that ordering is the point — when the first priority is sitting with him, the other forty stop shouting with equal authority. From that quiet, a truer question emerges than “what is urgent?” It is: what is needed? If you could move only one thing forward today — one conversation, one decision, one piece of real work — which one would still matter in a month? You usually know. The many things will survive being second. The one thing rarely survives being tenth. Choose it before you open the inbox, and let it take the best hour you have. A day that moves the needed thing is a good day, whatever else goes unfinished. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, I am worried and upset about many things, and I confess I like the feeling of being needed by all of them. Sit me down first. Show me the one thing today actually requires, and give me peace about what must wait. <break time="1.1s" /> I will choose the one needed thing before I open the inbox, and give it my best hour. <break time="1.1s" /> Go do the needed thing, and let the many things wait their turn. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-w-time: On Time as a Gift. <break time="1.8s" /> Another week is gone and you can barely say where. Pause and hold today like something entrusted to you. <break time="1.1s" /> “Teach us to number our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom.” <break time="1.1s" />Psalm 90:12. <break time="1.1s" /> Founders talk about time the way misers talk about money — saving it, spending it, never having enough of it. But Scripture starts somewhere else: your days are not a possession running out; they are a gift being handed to you, one at a time, by Someone who numbered them before you drew breath. “Teach us to number our days” is not an invitation to panic about the shortness of life. It’s a prayer for wisdom — the settled ability to see a single day at its true value. A steward and a miser handle the same resource differently. The miser grips; the steward invests, and can even give some away without feeling robbed. That reframe changes a calendar. The hour with your kid is not stolen from the company. The unhurried conversation with a struggling teammate is not waste. And the focused morning on the work God gave you is not anxiety’s treadmill; it’s faithful use of a talent entrusted. You cannot make more time, but you were never asked to. You were asked to be found faithful with today. Number it. Spend it on purpose. It was given to you. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, every day I have ever lived came from your hand, and I have treated so many of them as raw material. Teach me to number my days rightly. Make me a steward of this one — generous, unhurried, and faithful. <break time="1.1s" /> I will spend today on purpose, as a steward of a gift and not an owner running out. <break time="1.1s" /> Go steward this day well, for it was counted and given to you by God. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-w-hustle: On the Myth of Hustle. <break time="1.8s" /> The voice says sleep is for the funded and rest is for later. Come listen to a different voice. <break time="1.1s" /> “Unless the Lord builds the house, the builders labor in vain. … In vain you rise early and stay up late, toiling for food to eat — for he grants sleep to those he loves.” <break time="1.1s" />Psalm 127:1–2. <break time="1.1s" /> Hustle culture preaches a simple gospel: outcomes are purchased with hours, and whoever sleeps least wins. It flatters you, because it makes everything depend on you. Psalm 127 dismantles it in two verses. The psalmist isn’t against building — he assumes you’ll build — but he calls the all-hours version of it vain, and then says something almost scandalous to a founder: God grants sleep to those he loves. Sleep, in this psalm, is not lost productivity. It’s a nightly sermon, preached to your body, that the world is held together by Someone else. The myth of hustle isn’t wrong because hard work is bad; seasons of real push are part of building anything. It’s wrong because it quietly crowns you the sole load-bearing wall of your company, and no human soul is engineered for that weight. You can work hard tomorrow precisely because you are not God tonight. Deals have closed while founders slept. Ideas have arrived in the shower, not the sprint. Do your full day’s work, honestly and well — then put it down, and let the Builder keep building while you rest. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, I confess I’ve believed that everything depends on my grind. Unless you build this, I labor in vain. Teach me to work hard and then stop, and to receive sleep as your gift rather than my defeat. <break time="1.1s" /> I will do a full day’s honest work and then put it down, trusting the Builder with the night. <break time="1.1s" /> Go work hard and sleep well, for the Lord builds while you rest. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-w-finishing: On Finishing What You Start. <break time="1.8s" /> The exciting part is over and only the finishing is left — the unglamorous miles where most things quietly die. <break time="1.1s" /> “Now finish the work, so that your eager willingness to do it may be matched by your completion of it, according to your means.” <break time="1.1s" />2 Corinthians 8:11. <break time="1.1s" /> Starting is intoxicating. The blank repo, the fresh deck, the whiteboard full of possibility — beginnings run on inspiration, and inspiration is cheap. Finishing runs on something costlier. The Corinthians had eagerly pledged a gift and then let it stall, and Paul’s counsel is bracingly practical: let your completion match your willingness. He’s naming a gap every founder knows — between the enthusiasm that starts things and the fidelity that ships them. Your half-done projects aren’t failures of talent; they’re usually the moment when the work stopped feeding your excitement and started requiring your faithfulness. But notice the mercy in Paul’s phrase “according to your means.” God is not demanding a heroic finish beyond what you have. He’s asking you to close the loop with what is actually in your hands — the feature at ninety percent, the hire half-onboarded, the hard conversation opened and never landed. Shipping is a form of keeping your word, to your customers and to your earlier self. Pick one unfinished thing this week and carry it all the way across the line. Done, it can finally serve someone. Almost done, it serves no one. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, I am quick to begin and slow to complete. Forgive the trail of almost-finished things behind me. Give me the humble endurance of the last mile, and help me ship what I said I would. <break time="1.1s" /> I will take one nearly-finished thing all the way across the line this week. <break time="1.1s" /> Go finish the work, so your completion matches your willingness. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-w-margin: On Margin. <break time="1.8s" /> Look at your calendar: wall-to-wall color, not one blank hour. Even Jesus looked at days like that and said, come away. <break time="1.1s" /> “Come with me by yourselves to a quiet place and get some rest.” <break time="1.1s" />Mark 6:31. <break time="1.1s" /> Jesus said this on a day when so many people were coming and going that his team had no chance even to eat. It was, by any founder’s measure, traction — demand exceeding capacity, the mission working. And his response to that momentum was to schedule white space. We treat margin as the leftover, the slack we’ll enjoy once things calm down. But a page printed edge to edge is unreadable, and a life scheduled edge to edge is unlivable — there’s no room for the unexpected customer crisis, the teammate who needs twenty unhurried minutes, the idea that only surfaces when you’re not producing. Margin isn’t the enemy of productivity; it’s the condition for the kind that lasts. An engine at redline makes impressive noise and doesn’t last the year. Notice, too, that Jesus doesn’t send the disciples off alone; he says come with me. The quiet place isn’t just recovery — it’s company with him, the kind you can’t keep at a sprint. So put white space on the calendar with the same seriousness you give a board meeting. It is not empty. It’s where the best of you gets restored. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, my week has no room in it, and I have called that success. Teach me to guard margin the way I guard revenue. Draw me into the quiet place with you, and restore what the pace has worn thin. <break time="1.1s" /> I will block real white space in this week’s calendar and defend it like a commitment. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and keep some blank space in your days, for that is where you will hear him. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-w-from-rest: On Working from Rest. <break time="1.8s" /> You keep telling yourself you can rest once the work is done. But the work of a founder is never done — so the rest never starts. <break time="1.1s" /> “There remains, then, a Sabbath-rest for the people of God; for anyone who enters God’s rest also rests from their works, just as God did from his.” <break time="1.1s" />Hebrews 4:9–10. <break time="1.1s" /> Most founders work for rest: push through the sprint, close the round, hit the milestone — and then, finally, exhale. Except the exhale keeps moving. There is always a next milestone, so rest becomes a country you’re always emigrating toward and never reach. Scripture runs the sequence the other way around. In Genesis, humanity is created on the sixth day, which means our first full day of existence was God’s day of rest — we woke up into completion we hadn’t earned. Hebrews makes the pattern explicit: entering God’s rest means resting from your own works as the ground of your standing. That is the gospel applied to a calendar. You are not laboring toward acceptance; you are laboring from it. The verdict on you was settled at the cross, not at the quarter’s close. This changes the texture of a workweek more than any productivity system. Work done to earn rest is anxious, grasping, impossible to put down. Work done from rest can be bold, generous, and finished at a reasonable hour — because nothing ultimate is riding on it. Begin today already accepted. Then go build. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, I have been working to earn a peace you already gave me. Settle my heart in what is finished before I touch what is unfinished. Let me build from your rest today, not toward it. <break time="1.1s" /> I will start today from acceptance already given, not work toward a rest I must earn. <break time="1.1s" /> Go to your work from his rest, as one already loved and already received. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-w-today: On Doing Today’s Work Today. <break time="1.8s" /> Half your mind is on next quarter, next raise, next risk. Bring it back to the one day you’ve actually been given. <break time="1.1s" /> “Therefore do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about itself. Each day has enough trouble of its own.” <break time="1.1s" />Matthew 6:34. <break time="1.1s" /> A founder’s mind lives in the future by trade — modeling scenarios, gaming out the raise, rehearsing the churn that hasn’t happened yet. Some of that is planning, and planning is wisdom. But there’s a point where planning curdles into pre-suffering: you carry tomorrow’s troubles today, without tomorrow’s grace, because grace, like manna, is given a day at a time. Jesus’ instruction is strikingly concrete: each day has enough trouble of its own. He isn’t promising an easy tomorrow; he’s pointing out that you’ve been issued exactly one day of strength, and it’s for this one. The practical shape of that trust is almost embarrassingly simple — do today’s work today. Write the code in front of you. Make today’s calls. Solve the problem that actually exists rather than the six that might. You will handle next month’s crisis next month, with resources that haven’t been given yet and help you can’t currently see, because the Father who feeds you today will still be there when tomorrow becomes today. Anxiety splits you between two days and does justice to neither. Faith gathers you into one. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, I keep living a week ahead of my own life. Forgive my borrowing of troubles you haven’t assigned to me. Give me this day’s bread and this day’s work, and I will leave tomorrow in your hands. <break time="1.1s" /> I will do today’s work today and leave tomorrow’s troubles for tomorrow’s grace. <break time="1.1s" /> Go live this one day fully, and let tomorrow wait for you in the Father’s hands. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
payroll: For Not Making Payroll. <break time="1.8s" /> Before you open the spreadsheet again, open your hands. Breathe. The weight you carry was never meant to be carried alone. <break time="1.1s" /> “So do not worry, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ … your heavenly Father knows that you need them. But seek first his kingdom and his righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well.” <break time="1.1s" />Matthew 6:31–33. <break time="1.1s" /> You feel the names. Not numbers — names. The people who trusted you with their mortgages and their groceries. That weight is holy; it means you have not stopped caring. But the provider of this company is not you. You are a steward, not the source. The God who has carried you to this exact, narrow place is not surprised by the balance, and he has not handed you these people only to abandon you with them. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, I am afraid, and I bring the fear to you instead of pretending it away. You see the shortfall. You see the faces I am responsible for. I cannot manufacture what is not here. So I ask plainly: provide. Make a way I cannot see. And if the way is hard, give me the honesty to lead through it with integrity, and the courage to make the calls I am dreading. <break time="1.1s" /> I am a steward, not the source. I will do the next right thing, and I will trust the One who feeds the birds. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and do what is honest. You are not your bank balance. You are held. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
out-of-cash: For the Fear of Running Out. <break time="1.8s" /> It is late, or it is early, and the numbers are running on a loop. Stop the loop for five minutes. Let this be the quietest thing you do today. <break time="1.1s" /> “Do not be anxious about anything, but in every situation, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God. And the peace of God, which transcends all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.” <break time="1.1s" />Philippians 4:6–7. <break time="1.1s" /> Fear is a liar with a calculator. It takes today’s shortage and multiplies it out to a ruin that has not happened and may never happen. Scripture does not tell you to stop counting; it tells you to count differently — to set every petition beside thanksgiving, so the ledger of your fears always sits next to the ledger of God’s faithfulness. Look back. You have been in tight places before. You are still here. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, I have been doing math that only multiplies my dread. Quiet the loop. I give you the runway and the unknowns at the end of it. Guard my mind tonight. Tomorrow, give me one clear step, and the discipline to take it without panic. <break time="1.1s" /> I will not borrow tomorrow’s trouble. Today has enough grace in it. <break time="1.1s" /> May the peace that makes no sense stand guard at the door of your mind tonight. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
lost-deal: For the Deal That Fell Through. <break time="1.8s" /> You had already spent it in your mind — the relief, the next hire, the proof. Let your grip loosen on the thing that didn’t come. <break time="1.1s" /> “In their hearts humans plan their course, but the Lord establishes their steps.” <break time="1.1s" />Proverbs 16:9. <break time="1.1s" /> A lost deal is a small grief, and small griefs deserve honesty too. You are allowed to be disappointed. But a closed door is not always a punishment — sometimes it is protection you cannot yet read. Your worth was never riding on this signature. The “no” tells you about one outcome; it does not tell you about your calling, your competence, or your standing before God. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, I wanted this one. I am letting myself feel the loss instead of rushing past it. Establish my steps even when my plans collapse. Keep me from bitterness toward the people who said no, and keep me from despair. Show me what is next. <break time="1.1s" /> My steps are established by God, not by any single yes. <break time="1.1s" /> Go gently. The next door is already being prepared. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
want-to-quit: For When You Want to Quit. <break time="1.8s" /> You are tired in a way sleep doesn’t fix. Don’t make a forever decision from inside a hard week. Just be here for five minutes. <break time="1.1s" /> “Let us not become weary in doing good, for at the proper time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up.” <break time="1.1s" />Galatians 6:9. <break time="1.1s" /> There is a difference between a calling that is finished and a soul that is depleted, and exhaustion makes them look the same. Elijah, after his greatest victory, sat under a tree and asked to die. God’s first response was not a sermon — it was a meal and a nap. Maybe what you need to quit is not the work but the pace, the self-reliance, the lie that it all depends on you. Rest first. Decide later. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, I am running on empty and I have been pretending I’m fine. I don’t know if I’m meant to push through or lay something down — but you do. Restore me before I decide anything. Feed me. Quiet me. And in your time, make the way forward clear. <break time="1.1s" /> I will rest before I decide. Weariness will not write my future. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and rest without guilt. Even the strongest prophets needed bread and sleep. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
terrible-client: For a Terrible Client. <break time="1.8s" /> Before you reply to that message, set the phone down. Five minutes here will protect a relationship — or your integrity — out there. <break time="1.1s" /> “If it is possible, as far as it depends on you, live at peace with everyone.” <break time="1.1s" />Romans 12:18. <break time="1.1s" /> Notice the limits in that verse: “if it is possible” and “as far as it depends on you.” You are not commanded to make a difficult person reasonable — only to keep your own side of the street clean. Their behavior is theirs to answer for. Your tone, your honesty, your refusal to be controlled by contempt — those are yours. You can hold a firm boundary and a soft heart at the same time. You can even, by grace, see a frightened or wounded person underneath the rudeness. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, this person is wearing me down. Keep me from returning insult for insult or letting resentment make a home in me. Give me words that are clear and kind and unafraid. Where I need to set a boundary, give me the spine to do it cleanly. And help me see them, even now, as someone you love. <break time="1.1s" /> I will guard my own heart and my own words. The rest is not mine to carry. <break time="1.1s" /> Go in peace that does not depend on their approval. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
business-partner: For Conflict With a Partner. <break time="1.8s" /> This one cuts deeper because you chose them. Before you rehearse the argument again, bring the wound here first. <break time="1.1s" /> “In your anger do not sin: Do not let the sun go down while you are still angry, and do not give the devil a foothold. … Be kind and compassionate to one another, forgiving each other, just as in Christ God forgave you.” <break time="1.1s" />Ephesians 4:26–27, 32. <break time="1.1s" /> Anger itself is not the sin — Scripture assumes you will feel it. The danger is what anger becomes when it is fed in the dark: a foothold, a case you build silently, a story where you are wholly right and they are wholly wrong. Real stories are rarely that clean. Before you decide what they did, ask honestly what you contributed. Forgiveness is not pretending it didn’t hurt; it is refusing to let the hurt become a permanent resident. You forgave once because you were forgiven first. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, I am angry, and some of it is righteous and some of it is just pride. Help me tell the difference. Don’t let me nurse this in silence until it hardens. Give me the courage for an honest, direct conversation — not a war, not avoidance. Soften me where I am self-righteous. Strengthen me where I have been too afraid to speak the truth. <break time="1.1s" /> I will not feed this in the dark. I will seek the truth and offer the grace I have been given. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and make peace before the sun goes down — for your sake as much as theirs. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
hiring: For Bringing Someone On. <break time="1.8s" /> You are about to change someone’s life and weave them into yours. Pause and treat the moment as the sacred thing it is. <break time="1.1s" /> “Whoever can be trusted with very little can also be trusted with much.” <break time="1.1s" />Luke 16:10. <break time="1.1s" /> A new hire is not a resource you are acquiring; they are a person you are inviting to spend their one life inside the world you are building. That is a stewardship in both directions. They are entrusting you with their gifts and their season; you are entrusting them with your mission and your customers. Lead in a way that, years from now, they will be glad they said yes. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, give me wisdom to choose well and grace to lead well. Help me see this person clearly — not just what they can do, but who they are becoming. Make me the kind of leader who is worthy of their trust. And may this work be good for them, not just good for me. <break time="1.1s" /> I will steward this person well. They are not a means to my ends. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and build a place where people flourish. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
letting-go: For Letting Someone Go. <break time="1.8s" /> If this were easy, something would be wrong with you. The weight you feel is your conscience working. Sit with it for a moment. <break time="1.1s" /> “Masters, provide your slaves with what is right and fair, because you know that you also have a Master in heaven.” <break time="1.1s" />Colossians 4:1. <break time="1.1s" /> You answer to a Master too. That truth cuts both ways: it means you must sometimes make the hard call the business requires, and it means you must make it the way you would want it made if you stood where they stand. Clarity is a kindness; dragging it out is not. Dignity is not optional. You can be both the steward who protects the whole and the human being who treats one person with mercy. Do not let the difficulty make you cold, and do not let your kindness make you evasive. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, this is heavy, and I don’t want it to stop being heavy. Give me clarity to do what is right for the company and compassion to do it with honor. Let me be truthful without being cruel, and kind without being false. Go before this person into whatever comes next, and provide for them beyond what I can. <break time="1.1s" /> I will tell the truth with dignity. I serve a Master too. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and do the hard, honest thing — and carry no shame for caring. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
closing-a-deal: For Closing a Deal. <break time="1.8s" /> Before you post it, celebrate it, or spend it — stop and say thank you. Gratitude is the only sane response to a gift. <break time="1.1s" /> “You may say to yourself, ‘My power and the strength of my hands have produced this wealth for me.’ But remember the Lord your God, for it is he who gives you the ability to produce wealth.” <break time="1.1s" />Deuteronomy 8:17–18. <break time="1.1s" /> This is the most dangerous kind of moment, because success quietly rewrites the story until you are the hero of it. You did work hard — that’s true and worth honoring. But the talent, the timing, the open door, the very breath in your lungs while you signed: gifts, all of them. The antidote to pride is not pretending you did nothing. It is remembering who gave you the ability to do anything at all. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, thank you. This is good, and I receive it as a gift from your hand, not a trophy from my own. Keep me grateful and keep me grounded. Let this win make me more generous, not more grasping. And help me steward what you’ve provided in a way that blesses others. <break time="1.1s" /> I worked, and you provided. The increase is from your hand. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and celebrate — with a grateful heart and an open hand. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
launching: For Launching. <break time="1.8s" /> Years, or months, or sleepless weeks have led to this. Before you hit publish, take one quiet breath that belongs only to you and God. <break time="1.1s" /> “May the favor of the Lord our God rest on us; establish the work of our hands for us — yes, establish the work of our hands.” <break time="1.1s" />Psalm 90:17. <break time="1.1s" /> Launching is an act of hope and an act of surrender at once. You have done what you can do; the rest — whether it lands, who it reaches, what it becomes — is no longer in your hands. That’s frightening, but it’s also freeing. Your job was to make something good and offer it honestly. The outcome belongs to a bigger story than your metrics dashboard. Whatever today’s numbers say, the faithfulness of the building was real. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, I offer you the work of my hands. Establish it if it is good; redirect it if it is not. Let it serve real people and meet real needs. Free me from measuring my worth by today’s response. Whatever happens, I have been faithful to make and to ship — and that is enough. <break time="1.1s" /> I have done the work; the outcome is yours. Establish what is good. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and launch with open hands. The work was worship. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
unexpected-success: For Success You Didn’t Expect. <break time="1.8s" /> The thing took off, and somewhere under the thrill is a strange vertigo. Steady yourself here for a moment. <break time="1.1s" /> “But who am I, and who are my people, that we should be able to give as generously as this? Everything comes from you, and we have given you only what comes from your hand.” <break time="1.1s" />1 Chronicles 29:14. <break time="1.1s" /> Sudden success has its own temptations: to believe you finally are who the praise says you are, or to clutch the win in fear that it will vanish. King David, at the height of his nation’s wealth, responded not with a victory lap but with a question — “who am I?” — and an offering. Abundance is safest in the hands of someone who remembers it isn’t ultimately theirs. Let this be a moment of awe, not entitlement. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, this is more than I asked for, and it unsettles me as much as it delights me. Keep me humble in abundance the way I begged to stay faithful in scarcity. Don’t let success make me someone my family and team no longer recognize. Show me who to bless with what you have entrusted to me. <break time="1.1s" /> Who am I, that this should come to me? Everything comes from your hand. <break time="1.1s" /> Go in wonder, not entitlement. Hold the gift loosely and share it widely. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
morning: For the Morning’s Work. <break time="1.8s" /> The day has not started pulling at you yet. For these five minutes, give it to God before you give it to anyone else. <break time="1.1s" /> “Let the morning bring me word of your unfailing love, for I have put my trust in you. Show me the way I should go, for to you I entrust my life.” <break time="1.1s" />Psalm 143:8. <break time="1.1s" /> Whoever you listen to first tends to set the tone for the whole day. If the first voice is the inbox, you will spend the day reacting. If the first voice is the One who made you, you will spend the day rooted. The work matters, but it is not your master. You go into today not to prove your worth but to express it — already loved, already secure, already sent. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, before the noise, I want to hear you. Remind me I am yours before I am useful to anyone. Show me the way I should go today — what to say yes to, what to refuse, what to let go of. Make me a faithful steward and a steady presence.
